extracted.intended_audience: logicians, philosophers, scientists, and anyone designing precise scientific or philosophical terminology
extracted.subtask_description: Principles and practical rules for creating a language (terminology and nomenclature) suited to investigation and communication of truth — covering descriptive terms, names for abstractions, and names for Kinds. Emphasizes determinacy of meaning, fixed conventions for technical terms, and having names for things of scientific importance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determinate and unmistakeable meaning for each term
rubrics_metrics.description: Its terms shall each of them convey a determinate and unmistakeable meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dictionaries give broad/blunt senses and often fail to capture real usage and connotation; for a language adapted to investigation, words must have fixed, clear meanings so they do not mislead. Be alert to collateral associations and shades of meaning that dictionaries omit; where necessary define terms by the sense actually used.

rubrics_metrics.name: There should be no important meaning without its word
rubrics_metrics.description: Whatever we have occasion to think of often, and for scientific purposes, ought to have a name appropriated to it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For things or distinctions frequently encountered in observation or reasoning, provide a specific name rather than relying on circumlocution. This prevents loss of attention and facilitates expression, memory, and further reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accurate Descriptive Terminology for observations
rubrics_metrics.description: There ought to be all such names as are needful for making such a record of individual observations that the words of the record shall exactly show what fact it is which has been observed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Descriptive terminology must enable precise recording of individual facts; where possible provide names for elementary sensations and frequently recurring combinations so descriptions are exact rather than vague.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fix technical terms by convention and immediate association with perception
rubrics_metrics.description: The meaning of [descriptive] technical terms can be fixed in the first instance only by convention, and can be made intelligible only by presenting to the senses that which the terms are to signify... the term refers to the sensation, and not to the parts of the term.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teach technical terms by immediate exemplars (e.g., a color swatch for 'apple‑green') rather than by loose linguistic associations. Ensure the learner's memory associates the word directly with the perception it names so the term evokes the sensation without ambiguity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elementary sensations cannot be defined — require exemplars
rubrics_metrics.description: The names of elementary sensations, or elementary feelings of any sort, cannot be defined; nor is there any mode of making their signification known but by making the learner experience the sensation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For basic sensory or subjective terms, fix meaning through demonstration, standardized references, or shared examples rather than relying on verbal definitions that will be inadequate or ambiguous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use fixed, consistent senses for technical terms
rubrics_metrics.description: Always employ the same word in the same sense; fix the sense of terms so they always express the same idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt and maintain conventions (as in botanical or chemical nomenclature) so practitioners use terms uniformly. Where a term has both a general and a specific sense, keep the specific scientific meaning fixed and treat the popular sense as secondary or distinct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Introduce concise names for results of abstraction (inductive concepts)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whenever the comparison of a set of phenomena leads to the recognition in them of some common circumstance... this new conception ... should have a name appropriated to it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coin concise terms for important abstractions to fix attention and memory (examples: 'limit', 'momentum', 'civilization vs cultivation'). Short names facilitate reasoning and discovery by making complex ideas readily retrievable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide a nomenclature for every Kind
rubrics_metrics.description: There must not only be a terminology, but also a nomenclature... there shall be a name for every Kind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A 'Kind' is a class distinguished by a wide conjunction of properties; since Kinds will be the subjects of many predicates, assign specific names to them so they can be discussed and investigated as units.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employ standardized scales and classified measures where appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: Colour by means of a classified scale of colours... Werner's scale of colours... Mohs improved by giving a numerical scale of hardness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When properties admit ordinal or numerical comparison, adopt standard scales (e.g., color charts, Mohs hardness) to increase precision and comparability across observers and studies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use familiar or analogous names when introducing terms for new objects
rubrics_metrics.description: It is natural to prefer giving to a new object a name which at least expresses its resemblance to something already known... the name of a species often becomes the name of a genus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To introduce new concepts, leverage established names to indicate resemblance (genus/species relationships) rather than inventing wholly opaque neologisms; this aids comprehension and the uptake of terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be aware of and avoid 'question‑begging names' and connotative fallacies
rubrics_metrics.description: The additional connotation... gives rise to the fallacy of 'question-begging names.' The property which we are inquiring whether a thing possesses or not, has become so associated with the name of the thing as to be part of its meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid using names that embed the contested property (e.g., using a loaded term that presupposes the conclusion). Where such connotation exists irrevocably, define terms explicitly in the context of argument to prevent sleight‑of‑hand reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: When meanings irrevocably change, define according to new use and retain former senses as secondary
rubrics_metrics.description: The logician... should submit to them with a good grace when they are irrevocably effected, and if a definition is necessary, define the word according to its new meaning; retaining the former as a second signification, if it is needed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that ordinary language evolves; if a word's common meaning shifts, update formal definitions to match prevailing use and, where useful, record prior meanings as alternate senses rather than insisting on archaic usage.
